name: Regnault B mastopexy

card.summary: A breast-lift technique that uses a B-shaped incision pattern to raise the breast and nipple and reshape the chest contour with fewer scars than the anchor pattern.
card.note: Surgical procedure with permanent scars; complication risks rise with smoking, diabetes and obesity.

quick.overview:
The Regnault B technique is a way of performing a breast lift (mastopexy). The surgeon removes excess skin and repositions the nipple-areola complex through an inverted B-shaped incision, which proponents say avoids the medial vertical scar of the classic anchor pattern.

People seek it to restore a lifted, more youthful breast contour after pregnancy, weight loss or implant removal. A 2007 retrospective series of 40 women reported no medical complications and satisfaction in all patients, though large comparative trials are not described.
quick.how: It is performed by a plastic surgeon under anesthesia, sometimes combined with augmentation or liposuction. Scars take roughly a year to mature, and the vertical closure is described as about 5 to 7 cm.
quick.risks: General surgical risks include bleeding, infection and anesthesia effects; specific ones include nipple or skin necrosis, altered sensation, seroma, hematoma, wound separation and asymmetry. Smoking, diabetes, obesity and aspirin use are listed as contraindications or risk factors, and combined lift-augmentation carries higher complication rates.

lead: The Regnault B technique is a mastopexy (breast lift) variant, described by Regnault in 1974 for reduction mammaplasty, that uses an inverted B-shaped curvilinear incision. It lifts the breast and moves the nipple-areola complex to a higher position, giving a more youthful, projecting chest contour.[1]

It is classed among circumvertical approaches. Proponents say it removes the medial vertical scar of the anchor (Wise-pattern) lift, leaving fewer scars and rarely needing revision; it can be combined with augmentation or microliposuction.[1] The same article's grading of ptosis (Regnault grades I to IV, by nipple position relative to the inframammary fold) is often used to decide which lift is suitable.[1]

Published evidence includes a 2007 retrospective study of 40 women by Peterson and Tobin, reported to show no medical complications, one scar revision and universal satisfaction.[1] A German review also describes the 'modified B technique' as a tumour-adapted mastopexy in breast-conserving cancer surgery.[2]

chain: Excess skin removed through B-shaped incision
Nipple-areola complex and tissue repositioned higher
Lifted, more projecting breast contour with a shorter scar pattern
angle.text: The procedure physically raises and reshapes sagging breast tissue, which people seek after pregnancy, weight loss or implant removal. Its stated advantage is a scar pattern without the medial vertical limb of the anchor lift.

paras: The B technique uses a curvilinear incision shaped like an upper-case B. Because it limits the pattern to a circumvertical design, it is promoted as avoiding the medial vertical scar seen in the anchor pattern.[1] Indications for mastopexy generally include sagging after pregnancy, breastfeeding, menopause or major weight loss, ptosis after implant removal, congenital ptosis or tuberous breast deformity, and ptosis after mastectomy reconstruction.[1]

According to the Wikipedia mastopexy article, Regnault described the B technique for reduction mammaplasty in 1974, published the ptosis definition and grading in 1976, and a five-year B mastopexy experience was reported in 2007.[1]

General risks are bleeding, infection and anesthesia effects. Specific risks include skin or nipple necrosis, temporary or lasting sensory changes, seroma, hematoma, wound dehiscence, contour irregularity and asymmetry. Combined mastopexy-augmentation has higher complication rates than either alone, and aspirin use, smoking, diabetes and obesity are linked to nipple necrosis.[1] Scars fade but remain visible, with full maturation taking about a year.[1]

The reported series is the 2007 Peterson and Tobin retrospective review of 40 women, with no medical complications, one scar revision and satisfaction in all patients.[1] A 2016 review describes the modified B technique as a tumour-adapted mastopexy/reduction option that combines oncologic needs with symmetrical cosmetic results in breast-conserving surgery.[2]

timeline.event: Regnault describes the B technique for reduction mammaplasty.[1]
Regnault ptosis definition and grading published.[1]
